title: Theoretical Foundations of Neural Scaling Laws: Compute-Optimal Allocation, Multi-Modal Generalization, and Predictability of Emergent Capabilities
background:
Neural scaling laws have emerged as a cornerstone empirical framework for understanding how loss decreases predictably with model size, dataset size, and compute budget. The Chinchilla paradigm [1] established that compute-optimal training requires roughly proportional scaling of parameters and tokens, overturning earlier prescriptions and reshaping frontier model design. Subsequent work has connected these power-law exponents to data manifold dimension, kernel spectra, and feature learning dynamics [2][3], while solvable models in the infinite-width and high-dimensional limits have begun to derive scaling exponents from first principles [4]. Despite this progress, the theoretical foundations remain fragmented: existing analyses typically assume single-modality, i.i.d. data, fixed architectures, and smooth loss landscapes, none of which hold for modern foundation models trained on heterogeneous web-scale corpora.

Three gaps are particularly acute. First, compute-optimal scaling laws are derived under idealized assumptions and break down under realistic constraints such as data repetition, curriculum effects, and inference-time compute trade-offs [5]. Second, multi-modal training (vision-language, audio-text, embodied data) exhibits cross-modal transfer and interference effects that no current theory predicts; naive concatenation of unimodal scaling laws fails empirically [6]. Third, emergent capabilities, abilities that appear discontinuously at threshold scales, remain poorly understood: it is debated whether they reflect genuine phase transitions, metric artifacts, or latent continuous progress, and no predictive theory exists for when a given capability will emerge. Closing these gaps is essential for principled allocation of NSF-scale compute investments and for the scientific legitimacy of ML as a predictive discipline.
challenges: Deriving compute-optimal scaling exponents from first principles for non-i.i.d., repeated, and curriculum-structured data, including provable bounds on the Chinchilla-optimal ratio under data constraints and inference-compute trade-offs

Formulating a unified multi-modal scaling law that accounts for cross-modal transfer, modality competition, and tokenizer-induced effective-dimension mismatches, with falsifiable predictions on mixed vision-language-audio corpora

Establishing a rigorous theory distinguishing genuine emergent phase transitions from metric-induced discontinuities, including identifiability conditions and predictive estimators that forecast emergence thresholds from sub-scale measurements

Connecting microscopic feature-learning dynamics (e.g., neural tangent kernel evolution, mean-field limits) to macroscopic power-law exponents in a way that yields architecture-dependent and data-distribution-dependent corrections

Developing finite-sample, non-asymptotic generalization bounds that recover empirically observed scaling exponents rather than vacuous worst-case rates, and that extend to autoregressive and diffusion objectives
